newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Chirac pledges computer, literacy drive.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac pledges computer, literacy drive.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac, taking a leaf out of U.S. President Bill Clinton's book, called on Monday for a major drive to equip France's schools with computers and eradicate illiteracy to boost youth employment.

In a live television programme, Chirac said he wanted all secondary schools to be connected to the Internet by the year 2000 to develop computer skills and improve job prospects linked to information technology.
He sought to boost the morale of young people haunted by the prospect of employment.

Contrary to widespread belief, Chirac said, France was not behind its Western partners in computers. It had been ahead of others in developing the Minitel information network in the 1980s, but the time had come to take the next leap forward.
"I want by the year 2000, that is to say in three years' time, all secondary schools to be connected to information networks, and that will happen," he said.

Citing Clinton's plan to computerise U.S. schools and fight illiteracy, he said his aim was to eradicate illiteracy among French children entering high-school by the end of his seven-year term in 2002.
Chirac also said he had asked the government to cut value added tax on multimedia products and services, including CD-ROMs, to the lowest rate of 5.6 percent from 20.6 percent.

In contrast to a widely criticised television interview he gave in December, in which he blamed the French people's innate conservatism for economic stagnation, he sought to project optimism about France's dynamism, setting the stage for next year's general elections.
He denounced what he called "a sort of permanent masochism we have that stresses the negative and gives the impression there's no way forward".

Chirac said that France's 25 percent unemployment rate among 18 to 25 year-olds -- twice the national average for adults -- was unacceptable and could only be overcome by education, vocational training, career guidance and information technology.
"A nation can only be great if it integrates its young people," the president said.

In the past week the centre-right government has been buffeted by car-maker Renault's decision to close a Belgian plant and lay off 3,100 workers. France's opposition Socialists have pledged to find work for 700,000 young people if elected.

French media described the 105-minute programme, broadcast live from Paris's Science City against a backdrop of a gleaming geodesic dome, as an attempt to boost Chirac's standing among young people who voted disproportionately for him in 1995.
The tabloid daily Le Parisien dubbed it "Operation Reconquest", noting that young people were the hardest-hit victims of economic gloom.
Even the show's title "The year 2000, a chance for all?" echoed Chirac's presidential campaign slogan: "France for all".

An opinion poll published by the newspaper Le Journal du Dimanche showed young people had more confidence in themselves (65 percent) or their parents (40 percent) than in the president (13 percent) to "prepare their future and that of our society".
Half the 807 people questioned said the word "unemployment" was the best term to describe the Chirac generation, followed by the words "condom", "Internet" and "X-Files".
Chirac has criss-crossed the country recently to visit job initiatives for the young. Last week, he met company bosses from across France to discuss training and apprenticeships.
